Computing Consumer Tech Space & Aerospace Earnings Menu Money & Markets Economic Indicators Markets Personal Finance Earnings Menu Lifestyle Cars & Bikes Collecting Entertainment Food & Fine Dining Health and Fitness Real Estate Travel General Trivia How Armistice Day became Veterans Day: 8 turning points, 1918 to 1954 
 Veterans Day history starts with a 1918 armistice signed in a French railway carriage. Eight turning points trace how Armistice Day became a holiday for all veterans
 1 / 10 List slides How Armistice Day became Veterans Day: 8 turning points, 1918 to 1954 List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 5, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 The name on the calendar changed because the people the day honored changed. Nov. 11 began as a marker for the end of one war. Over 36 years, it became a day for every American who served in uniform.
 The date comes from the ceasefire. Under the World War I armistice, fighting on the Western Front was set to stop at 11 a.m. Paris time on Nov. 11, 1918. That hour and that day held. They shaped how Americans first marked the war's end, and they still set the holiday's place on the calendar.
 What followed was not a single decision. Veterans Day history is a sequence of steps taken by presidents, Congress and private citizens, each building on the last. A presidential proclamation gave the first anniversary official standing. A burial at Arlington National Cemetery gave the day a national ceremony and a fixed place. Congress first asked the president for yearly proclamations and later wrote the holiday into law. That law dedicated Nov. 11 to the cause of world peace under the name Armistice Day.
 By the 1940s, the country's veteran population had changed. World War II and the Korean War added millions of American veterans. A holiday tied by name and purpose to World War I did not reflect everyone who had served. In 1947, a World War II veteran organized a National Veterans Day observance in Birmingham, Alabama, and later lobbied for a holiday honoring all veterans. In 1954, President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the bill that renamed the day.
 That shift explains the holiday's meaning today. Memorial Day, observed in May, honors Americans who died in military service. Veterans Day honors everyone who served, living and dead. The date moved to the fourth Monday in October starting in 1971 and returned to Nov. 11 starting in 1978.
 The eight turning points below are a selection, not a complete account. They follow the holiday in chronological order, from a railway carriage in a French forest to a federal law signed in 1954. Each one stands on its own, and together they show how a ceasefire hour became a national day of recognition.
 The armistice signed at Compiègne on Nov. 11, 1918 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Germany and the Allies signed the armistice that ended the fighting of World War I inside a railway carriage in the Compiègne forest in France. The agreement set the guns on the Western Front to fall silent at 11 a.m. Paris time on Nov. 11, 1918.
 The carriage belonged to Marshal Ferdinand Foch, the French officer who served as supreme commander of the Allied armies. He led the Allied side at the talks. A German delegation headed by Matthias Erzberger, a civilian politician, traveled to the forest to receive the terms. The clearing sat northeast of Paris, behind the Allied lines.
 The document was signed in the early hours of that morning. The ceasefire did not take effect at the moment of signing. The parties fixed a later hour so the order could reach units spread across the front. Combat continued in the hours between the signatures and 11 a.m.
 An armistice is a halt to fighting, not a peace settlement. The terms required Germany to pull its forces out of occupied territory. Germany also had to hand over large quantities of weapons and equipment. The agreement ran for a fixed period and was renewed several times. The formal peace came later, with the Treaty of Versailles signed on June 28, 1919.
 That distinction shaped the holiday that followed. The date Americans would mark each year was not the day the war legally ended. It was the day the shooting stopped.
 The timing also gave the moment a durable shorthand: the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month. That phrase became attached to remembrance ceremonies in the U.S., the U.K., France and other countries. Many ceremonies still pause at 11 a.m. to mark it.
 The carriage itself kept a place in European history. In June 1940, Adolf Hitler had it brought back to the same clearing in the forest. France signed its armistice with Nazi Germany there, reversing the roles of 1918.
 For the American holiday, the main legacy of Compiègne is the calendar date. Nov. 11 became the anchor for the observances that later grew into Veterans Day.
 Woodrow Wilson's first Armistice Day proclamation, 1919 
 Illustration: Quartz
 President Woodrow Wilson marked the first anniversary of the armistice with a proclamation for Nov. 11, 1919. His message centered on two themes: solemn pride and gratitude for the victory that brought the war to a close.
 That pairing set the tone for the early observance. Wilson did not present the anniversary as a celebration of combat. He framed it as a time to honor the sacrifice behind the outcome and to give thanks that peace had returned. The emphasis fell on the end of the war rather than on the fighting.
 The first observance was also tied to the clock. The original plan for the day called for parades and public meetings. It also called for a brief pause in business beginning at 11 a.m., the same hour the ceasefire had taken effect a year earlier.
 The audience for the message had lived through the war directly. Many American service members had returned home only months before the anniversary. Families who had lost relatives in France were marking the date for the first time.
 A presidential proclamation is a formal statement that calls on the public to observe an occasion. It carries the authority of the office. It does not, by itself, create a permanent legal holiday. Wilson's 1919 message asked Americans to mark a single anniversary. It placed no obligation on future presidents or on Congress. Whether Nov. 11 would become a lasting national observance was still unsettled when the year ended.
 The proclamation came during a period of illness and political conflict for Wilson. He had suffered a stroke in early October 1919 and was still recovering when the anniversary arrived. In the Senate, the fight over the Treaty of Versailles was coming to a head.
 On Nov. 19, 1919, eight days after the first Armistice Day, the Senate voted against ratifying the treaty. The U.S. never joined the League of Nations, the international body Wilson had championed.
 The proclamation still gave Nov. 11 a presidential stamp in its first year. It also gave communities that chose to observe the date a shared language of pride and thanks.
 Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington, 1921 
 Illustration: Quartz
 On Nov. 11, 1921, an unidentified American service member from World War I was buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. President Warren G. Harding presided over the ceremony, held on the third anniversary of the armistice.
 The burial linked Nov. 11 to a permanent grave and a formal ritual. Arlington sits across the Potomac River from Washington. The tomb gave the anniversary a set location for official observance.
 The remains were chosen in France. Four unidentified American dead were exhumed from cemeteries there and brought to the city hall at Châlons-sur-Marne. Sgt. Edward F. Younger, a U.S. Army soldier who had served in the war, picked one of the four caskets in October 1921. He marked his choice by placing a spray of white roses on it.
 The chosen casket crossed the Atlantic aboard the USS Olympia. The cruiser had served as Commodore George Dewey's flagship at the Battle of Manila Bay in 1898. In Washington, the casket lay in state in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol. A procession then carried it to Arlington for the burial.
 The soldier's anonymity was deliberate. No name, rank, unit or hometown was attached to the remains. That allowed him to stand for every American who died in the war and was never identified. The tomb gave the families of those missing service members a place to mourn.
 The U.S. was not the first country to take this step. The U.K. buried its Unknown Warrior in Westminster Abbey on Nov. 11, 1920. France brought its own unknown soldier to the Arc de Triomphe in Paris that same day. The American burial followed a year later, on the same date.
 The tomb remains a site of national ceremony. Soldiers have guarded it around the clock since 1937. The changing of the guard takes place throughout the year. Each Nov. 11, the president or a representative traditionally lays a wreath there.
 That pairing of a date and a grave was part of Armistice Day observance years before Congress made the day a legal holiday in 1938.
 Congress's 1926 resolution on Armistice Day proclamations 
 Illustration: Quartz
 In 1926, Congress passed a resolution asking the president to issue a proclamation every year calling on Americans to observe Nov. 11. The measure did not create a holiday. It put Congress on record in support of an annual national observance of the armistice that ended the fighting of World War I.
 The resolution came eight years after the fighting stopped on the Western Front. By then, Nov. 11 already carried meaning for many Americans. What it lacked was a settled place in federal practice.
 A resolution and a statute do different work. A statute is a law. It can set a legal public holiday, change how federal offices operate and bind the government to act. A resolution of this kind expresses the view of Congress. It can urge, request or recommend. It cannot add a holiday to the federal calendar.
 That difference shaped what happened next. After the 1926 resolution, Nov. 11 was still not a legal federal holiday. The resolution's reach stopped at asking the president to act.
 A proclamation asks rather than orders. Its force rests on persuasion, not legal requirement. That made the 1926 measure a request for a request. Congress urged the president, and the president would in turn urge the public.
 Before 1926, whether to issue an Armistice Day proclamation was left to each president. The resolution added a standing request from Congress to that choice. Each November, a president issuing the call could point to the backing of the legislative branch.
 The yearly rhythm gave Nov. 11 continuity. A single proclamation marks one anniversary. A recurring one signals that the date is meant to be remembered every year, not only in the years closest to the war.
 The 1926 measure sat between custom and law. Official observance of Nov. 11 had begun with Woodrow Wilson's 1919 proclamation, seven years earlier. Making the day a legal public holiday would require a separate act of Congress, which came later.
 The 1938 law making Armistice Day a federal holiday 
 Illustration: Quartz
 An act of Congress dated May 13, 1938, made Nov. 11 a legal public holiday in the U.S. The law dedicated the day to the cause of world peace and set its name as Armistice Day.
 The law came 20 years after fighting stopped on the Western Front in 1918. Before it, federal observance of Nov. 11 rested on presidential proclamations rather than a permanent statute. The 1938 act changed that legal footing. The date no longer depended on a president deciding each year to call for its observance.
 The act also tied the holiday to the calendar date itself. Nov. 11 stayed Nov. 11, so the day of the week shifted from one year to the next. The holiday remained the anniversary of the 1918 ceasefire rather than a floating date chosen for convenience.
 A legal public holiday under federal law has a defined reach. It covers federal government offices and federal employees, and it applies in the District of Columbia. It does not by itself require states, private employers or schools to close. States set their own holiday calendars through their own laws. Each state decides whether to include a federal holiday.
 The dedication sets out the day's purpose in the law's own terms. Congress tied Nov. 11 to world peace rather than to military victory. That choice matched the date's origin as the anniversary of a ceasefire. The name pointed back to the same event: the 1918 agreement that halted the fighting.
 Franklin D. Roosevelt was president when the act became law. The measure kept the holiday tied to one conflict, World War I, which the U.S. had entered in 1917. The name Armistice Day made no reference to later wars or to veterans as a broader group.
 That narrow scope soon met a new war. World War II began in Europe in September 1939, about 16 months after the act became law. The statute's wording did not change, and Nov. 11 remained Armistice Day under federal law until Congress later amended the act.
 How World War II and the Korean War widened the holiday 
 Illustration: Quartz
 World War II and the Korean War left the U.S. with millions of additional veterans who had no direct tie to the 1918 armistice. Their numbers created pressure to broaden Nov. 11 beyond the veterans of World War I.
 Armistice Day was built around a single conflict. Its date marked the day fighting stopped on the Western Front. Its federal status, set in 1938, came with a dedication to the cause of world peace. That framing fit a country that still called the 1914–1918 conflict the Great War.
 That name did not survive the next war. The U.S. entered World War II after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941. American forces fought in Europe, North Africa and the Pacific until 1945. The term World War I reflects that a second global war followed the first.
 Congress recognized the new generation of service members in law before that war ended. The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the GI Bill, offered benefits such as education and home loans to returning World War II veterans. Veterans of the new war became a distinct group in federal policy. The November holiday, however, still carried the name of the earlier ceasefire.
 The Korean War added another group. American troops fought on the Korean Peninsula from 1950 until an armistice was signed on July 27, 1953. That agreement halted the fighting, but no peace treaty followed. A holiday named for one armistice now coexisted with veterans of a war halted by a different armistice.
 The result was a gap between the holiday and the people it might honor. By name and by its 1938 dedication, Armistice Day still pointed back to 1918. The veteran population of the early 1950s drew from several wars. Millions of those veterans had served long after the ceasefire the holiday commemorated.
 Raymond Weeks and the 1947 National Veterans Day 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Raymond Weeks, a World War II veteran, organized a National Veterans Day observance in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1947. He later lobbied for a holiday honoring all American veterans, not only those who served in World War I.
 Weeks held his event while Nov. 11 was still Armistice Day on the federal calendar. The 1938 law that made the date a legal public holiday kept that name. The name pointed back to the end of World War I.
 That name did not reach veterans of later wars. Weeks was one of them. Americans who served in World War II had fought in a separate conflict, one that began long after the 1918 armistice. The Korean War had not yet begun when he held his event. A holiday named for 1918 recognized their service only indirectly.
 The title Weeks gave the Birmingham event signaled a broader aim. He called it a National Veterans Day, even though it took place in one Alabama city. The name claimed a national scope for a local event. The word "veterans" moved the focus from a single armistice to the people who had served.
 A city observance carried no legal force. It could not rename a federal holiday or change the purpose written into federal law. That required Congress to amend the 1938 act. Weeks' later lobbying for an all-veterans holiday aimed at that level of change.
 The Birmingham observance gave the idea a public form before it existed in law. It presented veterans as a single group to be honored together, regardless of which war they had served in. It also showed that a veterans' observance could be organized by a private citizen rather than by Congress or the president.
 Seven years separated the 1947 Birmingham event from the 1954 law that renamed Armistice Day as Veterans Day. That law rested on the same principle his event had used: a holiday for veterans of all American wars.
 The 1954 law renaming Armistice Day as Veterans Day 
 Illustration: Quartz
 President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed a bill on June 1, 1954, that amended the 1938 act behind Armistice Day. The change renamed the holiday Veterans Day and extended it to honor veterans of all American wars.
 Congress did not write a new holiday statute from scratch. It revised the existing 1938 law, which had made Nov. 11 a legal public holiday. The amendment swapped the word "Armistice" for "Veterans." The date stayed the same. The change fell on the name and on the group of people the day recognized.
 The old name pointed back to a single event: the ceasefire that ended fighting on the Western Front in 1918. The new name pointed to people instead. Veterans Day covered anyone who had served in the nation's wars. That meant veterans of World War I, World War II and the Korean War alike, rather than one generation of service members.
 Eisenhower came to the signing with a long military career behind him. During World War II, he commanded the Allied forces that invaded Western Europe, including the D-Day landings in Normandy in June 1944. He held the rank of five-star general. As president, he signed a law that widened a World War I commemoration to include the veterans of the war in which he had led troops.
 The renamed holiday stayed on Nov. 11 through 1970. A scheduling law changed that. The Uniform Monday Holiday Act, passed by Congress in 1968, moved Veterans Day to the fourth Monday in October starting in 1971.
 The October date did not last. A 1975 law returned Veterans Day to Nov. 11, starting in 1978. The holiday has fallen on that date every year since, whatever the day of the week.
 The return restored the tie between the holiday and the 11 a.m. ceasefire of 1918. The broader purpose set in 1954 stayed in place. Veterans Day still honors those who served in every American war, on the anniversary of the moment that first gave Nov. 11 its meaning.
